metadata.narrative: Compose a concise technical report sketching an experimental plan for deciding whether a modern vision-language model could stand in for human specialists when labeling medical images of skin lesions.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): iterative hybrid dense+sparse ClimbMix search + document fetch, strict-JSON cited sentence answers.

answer.text: This report sketches an experimental plan for testing whether a modern vision-language model (VLM) such as GPT-4V, LLaVA, or SkinGPT-4 can substitute for human specialists in labeling dermoscopic/clinical images of skin lesions.

Background: CNN-era work already showed deep learning matching dermatologists, e.g. the Stanford study (Esteva/Thrun) trained on ~129,450 images and matched 21 dermatologists on biopsy-confirmed images.
Newer multimodal LLMs extend this: GPT-4V and LLaVA can distinguish melanoma from benign nevi, and GPT-4V as a retriever identifies the correct condition from image+history ~85% of the time.

Objective 1 — Task definition: fix a concrete labeling task (binary malignant/benign, multiclass diagnosis, or ABCDE-feature annotation), since VLM studies vary from full diagnosis retrieval to feature-conditioned reasoning.
Objective 2 — Data/ground truth: use ISIC, HAM10000, PH2 plus prospective images with biopsy/histopathology as the accepted reference standard for pigmented lesions.

Stratify by diagnosis, difficulty, and Fitzpatrick skin type, since existing tools underperform on darker skin (17% accuracy in a Ugandan Fitzpatrick VI cohort) and datasets are tonally/geographically biased.

Objective 3 — Human baseline: recruit multiple blinded board-certified dermatologists plus novice/GP readers on the same images, mirroring the prospective Australian/Austrian AI-vs-specialist-vs-novice trial design.

Objective 4 — VLM configuration: test zero-shot, few-shot, naive chain-of-thought, and guideline-grounded CoT prompting, since naive CoT sufficed for retrieval but guideline-grounded CoT and multi-agent conversation were needed for accurate diagnosis.
Vary phrasing, background skin color, and feature-conditioning (holding one ABCDE feature fixed) to probe whether reasoning tracks clinically relevant cues.
Objective 5 — Metrics: report sensitivity, specificity, and AUC-ROC for VLM and human readers against the histopathologic reference standard per standard diagnostic-accuracy guidance.
Compute Cohen's kappa (Krippendorff's alpha for >2 raters/categories) for inter-rater and human-vs-model agreement beyond chance.

Use McNemar's test (exact/mid-p for small discordant counts) for paired VLM-vs-specialist/novice comparisons, pre-specifying a non-inferiority margin akin to the ±5–9 point margins used in the pigmented-lesion equivalence trial.
Objective 6 — Failure-mode analysis: test for spurious correlations, since models have keyed on irrelevant artifacts like surgical rulers in malignant-lesion photos rather than true morphology.
Quantify hallucination rate using frameworks like THRONE, which found ~20% of free-form VLM statements about images were hallucinated—critical for diagnostics.
Check for human-like shape bias vs. texture bias, since CNN/VLM vision encoders are texture-biased relative to humans, risking poor generalization under covariate shift.
Report calibration (reliability diagrams, evidential/uncertainty methods) alongside accuracy, since overconfident-but-wrong predictions are a known safety risk.

Objective 7 — Ecological validity: include a prospective clinical arm, since an AI algorithm superior in retrospective studies became significantly inferior to specialists in a real clinical scenario.

Consider a deferral/collaboration arm rather than pure substitution, per CoDoC, which showed learning when to defer between a locked AI and clinician can exceed either alone in breast-cancer and TB screening.

Measure how specialists' accuracy shifts when given correct vs. incorrect AI labels, since GP accuracy rose from 73.6% to 86.8% with correct AI advice but erroneous advice could mislead less-experienced clinicians.
Objective 8 — Explainability: pair accuracy with review of model rationales/saliency to check alignment with recognized dermoscopic criteria rather than spurious cues.

Objective 9 — Annotation-pipeline analogy: frame this within IR/NLP literature on LLMs replacing human annotators, which warns of model-family bias, misinformation gaps, and hallucination, favoring human-in-the-loop labeling.
Objective 10 — Regulatory framing: align with FDA Software-as-a-Medical-Device/CDS guidance, which generally treats diagnostic image AI as a device needing clinical validation and clearance.
Address liability explicitly (assistive vs. autonomous framing), since liability for AI-influenced errors currently tends to fall on the provider relying on assistive AI.
Given specialist scarcity and rising skin-disease prevalence, report throughput/cost metrics to assess feasibility for teledermatology triage.

Recommended design: a multi-arm blinded study (VLM-only, specialist-only, novice-only, VLM-assisted-human) with paired statistical tests, stratified by skin tone/lesion type, biopsy-confirmed ground truth, reporting accuracy, kappa, calibration, hallucination rate, and explainability as co-primary outcomes.

This design directly tests whether a VLM can 'stand in' for a specialist by requiring it to meet a pre-specified non-inferiority margin while passing bias, hallucination, and spurious-feature safety checks identified in the retrieved literature.
